title: Shelter
summary: Pick flat, dry ground, insulate from the ground first and keep the shelter small.

list: Flat, dry ground above flood level, with no dead trees or hanging branches overhead.
Avoid valley floors on cold nights (cold air pools there) and exposed ridgetops (wind).
Close to water and building material, but never in a dry wash.

blocks.cap: A level spot partway up a slope beats both the valley floor and the ridgetop.

steps: Insulate from the ground first: a bed of dry leaves, grass or boughs at least a hand’s width thick once you lie on it. The ground pulls heat out of you faster than the air.
Keep it small, just big enough to lie in. Your body has to heat the space.

Debris hut: prop a long ridgepole on a stump or forked stick at about hip height. Lean sticks along both sides, then pile leaves and debris at least an arm’s length thick. Pull a pile of leaves into the entrance once you’re inside.

Lean-to: lash a pole between two trees, lean branches against it on the windward side, and cover with boughs or a tarp. Build a fire in front, with a wall of logs or rocks behind it to reflect heat in.
Tarp: tie a ridgeline between trees and drape the tarp over it as an A-frame, low end facing the wind.

blocks.cap: Debris hut. More debris means more warmth; it should be thick enough that you can’t see light through it.
Lean-to. The log wall throws the fire’s heat back into the shelter.
Tarp A-frame. Pitch the end facing the wind lower to keep rain and wind out.

list: A snow trench or snow cave insulates well. Poke a ventilation hole, keep your digging tool inside with you, and never use a stove or fire in a sealed snow shelter.

blocks.cap: Snow trench. Sleeping above the floor keeps you out of the coldest air.
